title: A cellular automaton's class usually cannot be read off its rule

fields.label: Label
fields.value: A cellular automaton's class usually cannot be read off its rule

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: For most cellular automata there is no easy way to determine from the underlying rule which class of behavior it will produce; one generally has to run it and see, though some rule forms can be shown to give only class 1 or 2 behavior.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: In most cases there is no easy way to do this, and in fact there is little choice but just to run the cellular automaton and see what it does.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 6, “Starting from Randomness”; section “Four Classes of Behavior” (from p. 231), p. 240. Scope: predicting cellular automaton behavior class from rule specification

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch06-05: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.66

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Predictive difficulty can be measured empirically in bounded families, and theory settles some special cases. The broad informal claim cannot be confirmed solely by current classifier performance.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fix a rule family, formal class labels, and resource bound for “easy,” then compare static rule-analysis algorithms against direct simulation on held-out rules. Complexity or undecidability results can establish stronger restricted impossibility statements.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Behavior class may depend on initial conditions.

Finite predictive failures do not prove impossibility.

“No easy way” depends on a computational model and resource bound.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The positive half, that some syntactic families never leave class 1 or 2, is a finite proof of the sort the text sketches and can be checked. The negative half, that most rules have no easy class readout, is an absence claim: public rule tables let one try predictors, and a strong predictor would hurt it, but unsuccessful trials leave it open. The two halves therefore resolve to different degrees.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Prove the syntactic restrictions that the text says yield only class 1 or 2, and separately train simple predictors from the rule table to the class on a held-out finite family. A predictor that is short and accurate on most of that family would challenge the no-easy-way clause; the syntactic proofs stand or fall on their own.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Failure of several predictors does not prove that no easy predictor exists.

Undecidability applies to infinite families, not to one fixed finite rule table.

Easy way is a family of formalizations, not a single test.
